title: ISRO Launches NVS-03 Successfully, Restoring NavIC to Full Working Strength
excerpt: GSLV-F18 placed the 2,232 kg navigation satellite in its intended orbit late on October 30, returning India's NavIC constellation to its four-satellite minimum and adding the smartphone-friendly L1 signal.
body:
• ISRO's GSLV-F18 lifted off from Sriharikota at 11:51 p.m. IST on October 30 and placed the NVS-03 navigation satellite in its intended orbit — mission success confirmed.
  • Chairman V. Narayanan said the launch restores NavIC to its minimum operational configuration of four satellites.
  • NVS-03 adds the L1 signal used by smartphones, alongside L5 and S-band, and carries an indigenous rubidium atomic clock.
  • The mission was flown just 56 days after the previous GSLV launch, ISRO's shortest turnaround between GSLV missions.

India's space agency ISRO successfully launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite on Friday night, restoring the NavIC constellation to its minimum operational configuration. The GSLV-F18 rocket lifted off from the Second Launch Pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota at 11:51 p.m. IST on October 30 and placed the satellite in its intended Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit, ISRO confirmed.

"Mission Success! GSLV-F18 has successfully placed NVS-03 in the intended orbit," ISRO announced. The roughly 2,232-2,250 kg satellite will now use its own propulsion for orbit-raising manoeuvres to reach its final geosynchronous slot at 32.5 degrees East, IANS reported.

"With the success of this launch, the NavIC constellation is restored to the minimum operational configuration with 4 satellites. NavIC constellation is a strategic national asset that provides the nation independent access to position, navigation and timing services."

— V. Narayanan, Chairman, ISRO

Why NVS-03 mattered

NavIC — Navigation with Indian Constellation — is India's independent regional navigation system, providing position, velocity and timing services over India and a region extending about 1,500 km beyond its landmass. ISRO told Parliament in July 2026 that only three NavIC satellites then supported positioning, with timing active. NVS-02, launched in January 2025, reached its transfer orbit but could not complete orbit-raising after a drive signal failed to reach a pyro valve in its oxidizer line. NVS-03, the third satellite in the second-generation NVS series, closes that gap.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=QkljvSH4ixk

The satellite also upgrades the service. It broadcasts the L1 navigation signal in addition to the existing L5 and S-band signals — L1 is the band most widely used by smartphone chipsets, which improves NavIC availability in consumer devices — and it carries an indigenous rubidium atomic clock alongside procured clocks. Five second-generation satellites are planned in total, according to ANI reporting of the launch.

A record-paced campaign

Narayanan said the GSLV-F18 mission flew just 56 days after the previous GSLV launch — the shortest interval ISRO has achieved between GSLV missions — with the launch campaign completed in 47 days and the rocket's four L40 strap-on boosters prepared in a record 37 days. GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of the GSLV family, a three-stage vehicle using solid, liquid and cryogenic propulsion, and ISRO's fifth orbital mission of 2026.

What happens next

NVS-03 must first complete its orbit-raising and in-orbit checks before its navigation payload enters service. NVS-04 and NVS-05 are in preparation to deepen the constellation further. Union Minister Jitendra Singh congratulated ISRO on X, calling the launch a reflection of India's growing space capability and its commitment to sovereign navigation — the system that keeps Indian positioning independent of the US GPS network.
